slides.title: How Web Apps Communicate

slides.title: How Web Apps Communicate
slides.body:
How Websites Remember Users?
REST rule
Every request is independent
server forgets the client after each request
But… users add items to cart, close the browser, come back next day → cart is still there
If the server forgets everything, how does this work?

slides.title: How Web Apps Communicate
slides.body:
How Websites Remember Users?
To answer this, there are two ways a server handles requests — Stateless vs Stateful

slides.title: Ways to Handle Client Interactions by Server
slides.body:
Stateless Communication
Stateless = random helpline agent each call
Server remembers NOTHING between requests
Each request carries full context (auth, data, everything)
Used by: HTTP, REST APIs, DNS
Pros
Highly scalable, any server handles any request
Cons
More data per request, feels "forgetful"

slides.title: Ways to Handle Client Interactions by Server
slides.body:
Stateful Communication
Stateful = dedicated account manager who knows your history
Server REMEMBERS previous interactions
Client sends only a reference (session ID), server recalls the rest
Used by: FTP, WebSockets, database connections
Pros
Less data per request, smoother UX
Cons
Harder to scale, server crash = data loss

slides.title: Cookies
slides.body:
What Are Cookies?
 Small pieces of data stored in the browser and sent with every request to the server.
Storing Session ID
Saving small preferences (theme, language)
Identifying users
uses

slides.title: Cookies
slides.body:
Limitations and Security Risks 
Security Risk: Can be stolen if not secured (e.g., no HTTPS encryption)
Data Limitation: Only stores small amounts (around 4KB)
Sensitive Data: Not suitable for sensitive info (e.g., passwords) use secure session identifiers and encryption

slides.title: Cookies
slides.body:
Cookie Types
Session Cookies (Temporary)
Session cookie
movie ticket (today only)
2.  Persistent Cookies (Long-Lasting)
Persistent cookie
season pass (valid for months)

slides.title: Cookies
slides.body:
1. Session Cookies (Temporary)
Deleted when browser closes
No Expires / Max-Age attribute set
Stored in RAM only (not on disk)
Use cases: shopping cart, temporary login, form navigation
More secure, no trace after browser closes
Example: Set-Cookie: sessionId=abc123

slides.title: Cookies
slides.body:
2. Persistent Cookies (Long-Lasting)
Survive browser restarts
Has Expires or Max-Age attribute
Written to disk (persistent storage)
Use cases: "Remember Me", theme/language prefs, analytics
Less secure — remains on disk, can be stolen
Example: Set-Cookie: theme=dark, 	         Max-Age=2592000 (30 days)

slides.title: Cookies
slides.body:
Security Attributes
Cookie sent ONLY over HTTPS, Prevents interception
Secure
JavaScript cannot access it, Protects against XSS
HttpOnly
Controls cross-site behavior:
Strict — Never sent cross-site (most secure)
Lax — Sent on top-level navigations only (default)
None — Sent always (requires Secure flag)
SameSite

slides.title: Cookies
slides.body:
Security Attributes
Which domains receive the cookie (e.g., .example.com = all subdomains)
Secure
Limits cookie to specific URL path (e.g., /api)
Set-Cookie: sessionId=xyz; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Path=/; Max-Age=3600
Path
Best Practice

slides.title: Sessions
slides.body:
What Are Sessions?
A session is like a temporary workspace on the server where the server keeps track of information about you (such as login status, shopping cart items, etc.) while you're using a website

slides.title: Sessions
slides.body:

slides.title: Sessions
slides.body:
Why Sessions Matter?
Continuity
Server remembers you across requests
Secure storage
Sensitive data stays on the server
Seamless interactions
Maintains shopping carts, settings, and preferences

slides.title: Sessions
slides.body:
Security Considerations
Use HTTPS: Encrypt data to prevent unauthorized takeover of the session.
Secure & HttpOnly Cookies: Protect against attacks (e.g., XSS)
Set Session Expiration: Timeouts or invalidate after logout
